title: Wendell and the House
premise: Urban explorer Lena Eastwick discovers unmapped tunnels beneath her late grandmother's house, and when an extra chair appears in every old family photograph, she realizes something was invited in decades ago — a presence called Wendell, bound by a bargain her grandmother made to keep the family safe. As the house begins claiming the living, Lena must choose between sealing the tunnels forever, which would trap her grandmother's lingering spirit, or renewing the bargain herself, which would corrupt her just as it corrupted Wendell, once a man who only wanted to belong. At sunrise, Lena breaks the cycle by un-inviting Wendell with love instead of banishment, freeing them both at the cost of the house itself.
about_author: Wren Galloway is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent years documenting structures that official records insisted did not exist. They write horror about houses that remember more than the people who lived in them.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. An urban explorer with a reputation for finding what maps miss, Lena crawls into a storm drain behind her grandmother's abandoned house and finds tunnels no survey acknowledges — warm, dry, and faintly lit from within. The beat is professional curiosity curdling into unease as her compass spins and her flashlight dims politely, as if asked.

chapters.title: Counting Doors
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Back inside the house, Lena counts eleven doors on a floor plan that should have ten, and keeps the lights burning because the dark feels attentive. She finds grandma's journal: rules, tallies, and one repeated line — 'the chair stays empty.' Emotional beat: inherited dread, the sense of walking into a job someone died doing.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Sorting photographs for the estate sale, Lena notices a wooden chair in every family picture across sixty years — including shots taken outdoors, where no chair was carried. In the newest photo, taken last week, someone sits in it, out of focus. Beat: the past reorganizing itself around an intruder.

chapters.title: Wendell
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. The journal names him: Wendell, invited in 1963 by great-grandfather to 'keep the cold out.' Grandma's entries grow desperate — Wendell wants to be family, not furniture. That night Lena hears a chair scrape upstairs. Beat: the intruder acquires a name, and names are invitations.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Lena and Wendell. For the first time we see through Wendell: he remembers being a drifter in 1963, hungry for a place at any table, and accepting terms he didn't understand. His chapters are tender and wrong. Beat: sympathy for the monster; corruption dressed as belonging.

chapters.title: The Tunnels Breathe
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. The tunnels under the house pulse like a throat; Lena follows them and finds rooms furnished in decades-old styles, each set for a meal, each with a chair pulled out waiting. She realizes the house isn't haunted — it's occupied. Beat: claustrophobic awe turning to resolve.

chapters.title: Grandma's Terms
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Decoding the journal, Lena learns grandma renewed the bargain yearly: keep the lights on, count the doors, leave the chair empty, and the family lives. Grandma missed a renewal while dying in hospice. The contract lapsed nine days ago. Beat: grief weaponized — the deadline is already passing.

chapters.title: First Claim
chapters.summary: POV of Marcus, Lena's brother, who arrived to help with the estate. He falls asleep in the extra chair and wakes changed — polite, helpful, wrong, humming a tune grandma used to sing. Lena watches her brother become a placeholder. Beat: the cost becomes personal and immediate.

chapters.title: Sunrise Rules
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Wendell appears at the kitchen table, courteous, and explains the mechanics: hold out until sunrise, refuse the chair, and the claim lapses. But Marcus is already half his. Lena negotiates — Wendell wants what he's always wanted: to be kept. Beat: horror negotiating as domestic negotiation.

chapters.title: The Long Evening
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, real-time. One night compressed: doors multiplying, lights failing room by room, Wendell setting the table for three. Lena keeps counting aloud to stay anchored. Marcus sets a fourth plate without being asked. Beat: endurance horror; love expressed as stubbornness.

chapters.title: False Dawn
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. A gray light floods the windows at what should be dawn — but the sun rises in the west. Wendell apologizes sincerely: time runs differently below. The first night never ended. Beat: despair; the rules themselves are part of the house.

chapters.title: Below
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. To end the night, she must reach where the bargain was signed — the deepest tunnel room, a replica of the 1963 kitchen. Wendell guides her down, almost gentle, warning her what she'll find. Beat: descent structured as trust; the monster as reluctant guide.

chapters.title: Great-Grandfather's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. In the replica kitchen she finds the original contract and evidence that great-grandfather didn't invite Wendell to protect the family — he invited him to replace a son who'd died, then tried to discard him when the grief passed. Wendell has been holding a grudge and a hope for sixty years. Beat: the origin reframed; power corrupted everyone.

chapters.title: Marcus Sits Down
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV, fragmenting. Fully claimed now, Marcus descends to take his seat at the table permanently. He narrates with serene happiness that horrifies more than fear would. Lena reaches him at the threshold. Beat: the stakes embodied; duty to family versus duty to truth.

chapters.title: The Renewal
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Wendell offers the pen: sign, take grandma's place, keep the lights on forever, and Marcus goes free. It's the same offer grandma accepted, the same corruption wearing a kinder face. Lena reads the contract fully for the first time — and finds the loophole grandma underlined and never used. Beat: temptation at its most reasonable.

chapters.title: The Loophole
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. The contract binds whoever is 'kept' by the house — but nothing says the keeper can't be un-kept with consent. Banishment fails because it's refusal; release might work because it's permission. Wendell has never been offered the door open rather than shut. Beat: hope built from empathy instead of force.

chapters.title: Un-Invited
chapters.summary: Lena and Wendell alternating POV. Lena stands at the threshold and tells Wendell he was never the monster — he was a grieving man's mistake, kept too long. She releases him formally, with the words of invitation reversed into words of farewell. Wendell hesitates at the door he hasn't fit through since 1963. Beat: climax of compassion; the hardest thing is leaving.

chapters.title: Sunrise, Real This Time
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Wendell steps out and dissolves into morning light, whispering thanks. The false night tears open; true dawn enters the kitchen. Marcus wakes in the chair, himself, remembering nothing but crying without knowing why. The tunnels exhale and go cold and ordinary. Beat: catharsis; the house becoming just a house.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Sealing the tunnels means burying grandma's spirit, still tethered below. Instead Lena performs a small funeral in the replica kitchen, thanks her grandmother aloud for thirty years of counted doors, and lets the tether go. The house settles. Beat: mourning completed; duty discharged with love rather than obligation.

chapters.title: Estate Sale
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Weeks later, the sale happens. Lena keeps only the journal and one photograph — the oldest one, where she's digitally removed the chair, and the picture finally looks like a normal family. Buyers ask if the house is haunted; Lena says it's just tired. Beat: quiet aftermath; memory curated honestly.

chapters.title: A Place at the Table
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Lena and Marcus share dinner in the emptied house before handing over the keys. She sets two places, then pauses, and sets a third — empty, on purpose, as remembrance rather than invitation. Nothing comes. Beat: reclaiming ritual; belonging chosen, not bargained for.

chapters.title: The Lights Stay On
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Lena's POV, epistolary close via her survey notes. Lena files a report on the tunnels that officially don't exist, marked 'sealed, do not reopen,' and drives away as the new owners turn on every light in the house — a habit they can't explain but keep anyway. Last line echoes grandma's journal: some lights you keep out of love, not fear. Beat: resolution with a warm, watchful shiver.
